items.prompt: Solve for x: 6x + 10 = 70
items.rationale: Subtract 10 to get 6x = 60, then divide by 6 for x = 10.

items.prompt: Line A has slope 2/3 and line B has slope -3/2. What is the relationship?

items.prompt: A linear function has f(1) = 12, f(2) = 18, f(3) = 24. What is f(4)?

items.prompt: Is x = 6, y = 5 a solution of the pair x + 4y = 26 and x + 3y = 21?
items.rationale: Substituting gives 1(6) + 4(5) = 26 and 1(6) + 3(5) = 21, which are both the right sides.

items.prompt: What is the positive square root of 16?

items.rationale: The slope is (-4 − (-3)) ÷ (7 − 0) = -1/7. Substituting (0, -3) into y = mx + b gives b = -3 − (-1/7)(0) = -3.

items.prompt: According to the passage, how much more did the gentler grade cost to operate?
items.rationale: The text states it "cost, in the end, almost four times as much to operate."
items.passage: The first survey of the ridge was commissioned in 1874, three years after the miners had already begun digging. The engineer argued for a summit tunnel and was outvoted by a party who preferred a long, gentle grade — a decision that cost, in the end, almost four times as much to operate and would cost a great deal more in the decades after the coal ran out. Work started in 1891. The western portal opened first, in 1904, and by then the company had spent more than it had twice over. The eastern portal met harder ground, flooded twice, and did not open until 1911. When the two ends finally joined, the tunnel was nearly twelve miles long. Traffic was heaviest in the years immediately after, and fell for four decades. The argument now is about what to do with it, and the two positions are not really about engineering at all.

items.prompt: The passage is primarily concerned with
items.answer: how the octopus nervous system complicates ideas about a single mind
items.rationale: Each example — the arm, the imitation, the stable preferences — feeds the closing question of whether the animal is one individual or a federation.
items.passage: An octopus has roughly five hundred million neurons, and about two-thirds of them sit outside its brain, distributed through its arms. This arrangement has consequences. An arm severed from the body will still reach toward food and pass it toward a mouth that is no longer there, which suggests the arm is running a program of its own rather than waiting for instructions. In laboratory tanks, octopuses learn to open jars, and they learn faster when they have watched another octopus do it first. They also appear to make decisions we would call arbitrary: given two equally good routes to the same shelter, individual animals show stable preferences that persist across weeks. Researchers disagree about what to call this. Some argue that a nervous system built on this plan cannot support a unified experience at all, and that the octopus is better described as a federation than as an individual. Others note that the same could be said, with less confidence than we usually manage, of us.
choices: the disagreement between two named research teams
why severed octopus arms continue to move
the process by which octopuses learn to open jars
how the octopus nervous system complicates ideas about a single mind
items.user_answer: the disagreement between two named research teams

items.prompt: The detail that the report "said so in one sentence and moved on" primarily serves to
items.answer: suggest that the comparison stretch had settled the question about reed warblers
items.rationale: Dismissing an objection in one sentence is what you do with an objection that no longer needs arguing, which is the effect the comparison site had.
items.passage:
For 9 years Hanne Vogel counted reed warblers at a salt marsh east of the river mouth, and for most of that time the figures barely moved: 93 nesting pairs in an average season, give or take a handful. The change, when it came, was not gradual. In the first season after the reed beds were cut back each autumn, the count fell to 23, and it stayed there the following year and the year after that. Hanne had expected some effect and found the size of it hard to credit: a 75 percent drop is not a bad season, it is a different site.

What made the case convincing was a second location. Eleven kilometres away, a stretch of the same habitat where the autumn cutting never happened held steady at 93 through the same three seasons. The weather was shared; the outcome was not. Against that comparison the objection that reed warblers simply have poor years everywhere looks flimsy, and the report published in the spring said so in one sentence and moved on.
choices: show that the finding was ignored
introduce new work on the autumn cutting
criticize the report for being too brief
suggest that the comparison stretch had settled the question about reed warblers
items.user_answer: suggest that the comparison stretch had settled the question about reed warblers

items.passage:
For 17 years Peter Nakamura counted wild bees at an abandoned orchard behind a disused rail line, and for most of that time the figures barely moved: 93 foraging visits in an average season, give or take a handful. The change, when it came, was not gradual. In the first season after a neighbouring farm switched to drip irrigation, the count fell to 14, and it stayed there the following year and the year after that. Peter had expected some effect and found the size of it hard to credit: an 85 percent drop is not a bad season, it is a different site.

What made the case convincing was a second location. Eleven kilometres away, a stretch of the same habitat where the irrigation change never happened held steady at 93 through the same three seasons. The weather was shared; the outcome was not. Against that comparison the objection that wild bees simply have poor years everywhere looks threadbare, and the report published in the spring said so in one sentence and moved on.
choices: necessary to rule out anything the orchard and the comparison stretch had in common
more important than the orchard itself
evidence that the wild bees will not return
items.user_answer: necessary to rule out anything the orchard and the comparison stretch had in common
